title: Invisible Editing
objective: After this level you can explain continuity editing and the match on action, which hide cuts so a scene feels unbroken.
summary: Continuity editing, classical Hollywood's 'invisible editing', matches direction, position and time across cuts. A match on action carries a movement across the cut.

cards.headline: A scene is full of cuts. So why doesn't it feel chopped up?
cards.body: A scene you watch is really a string of separate shots, joined by cuts. Yet a character crosses a room and it feels like one smooth moment, in one place, at one time. Somebody worked hard to keep it that way. Here's the system behind it.

cards.headline: Hollywood's invisible style
cards.body: From the 1930s to the 1950s, classical Hollywood's dominant style is sometimes called invisible editing, because its cuts are so unobtrusive. Its formal name is continuity editing: a system of cutting that keeps the action clear and continuous by matching screen direction, positions and time from shot to shot. It backs up an assumption you make without thinking: that space and time run on unbroken across every cut.

cards.headline: Cut in the middle of a move
cards.body: A favorite place to hide a cut is inside a movement. In a match on action, a movement begun in one shot is picked up where it left off in the next. A hand reaches for a cup, cut, and a closer shot finishes the reach. The movement stitches the two shots together, so you read one continuous gesture instead of a join.

cards.headline: The doorway that joins two places
cards.body: D. W. Griffith used the trick in the films he made at Biograph from 1908 to 1913. A character walks into a doorway outdoors, and in the next shot enters an interior built as a set. The outside and the inside were filmed in different places, but the matched step through the door makes them one house. The door is the stitch.

cards.headline: Invisible editing: seen
learned: Continuity editing matches direction, position and time
Match on action: cut mid-movement, continue it next shot
Griffith's doorway joined places filmed apart

questions.prompt: Why is classical Hollywood's continuity style sometimes called invisible editing?

options.label: Its films were edited without any cuts
options.rationale: Continuity films are full of cuts; they just hide them.

options.label: Its cuts are so unobtrusive you barely notice them
Its editors worked in darkened rooms
options.rationale: The name is about what viewers notice, not the editors' rooms.

options.label: Its editors' names never appeared in the on-screen credits
options.rationale: The name describes the cuts, not who was credited.

questions.explanation: Continuity editing keeps the cuts so unobtrusive that the action seems to run on without a break.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of this match on action in order, from first to last.
items: A hand reaches for a cup
A closer shot finishes the reach
questions.explanation: A hand reaches for a cup, the film cuts, and a closer shot finishes the reach, so you read one continuous gesture.

questions.prompt: Your brain supplies the motion between still frames. What does continuity editing count on you to supply between shots?

options.label: The missing frames hidden inside each separate shot
options.rationale: Each shot is complete; the question is what happens between shots.

options.label: Flicker fusion to hide the splice
options.rationale: Flicker fusion steadies flickering light; it does not join shots.

options.label: The dialogue the actors left out
options.rationale: Continuity editing is about space and time, not missing lines.

options.label: The sense that space and time run on unbroken

questions.explanation: Continuity editing supports your assumption that space and time continue unbroken from one shot to the next.
